rv.q: Although equipped with fertile material, Lapine falls short of sharpening the ideological and interpersonal tensions of An American Daughter.

Unfortunately, she’s ill-equipped for it, not only because she’s significantly older than the part calls for, something that proves highly distracting, but also because her vocally grating, one-note performance sucks the energy out of the evening.

rv.q: An actress with a limited vocal range, shaky diction, and a small presence, she has struggled with dramatic roles in Nora (Ingmar Bergman's take on A Doll's House ) and The Night of the Iguana.
This makes the core plot of “An American Daughter” feel less than timely.
Unfortunately, the play is too schematic to be convincing and without enough humor to carry the story to its logical ending.

What should be an evening of wittily sparkling chatter about personal and political concerns centering on the central character’s career dilemma is instead a surprisingly dull, flatly performed, talky exercise about issues that fail to engage us fully.
But it's bloated: too many subplots that don't amount to anything, and no way it has to drone on for over two and a half hours.
The current political climate, however, may not have been the right time to revive An American Daughter as all the play'
Funny without being frivolous, political without becoming didactic, and deeply compassionate without ever surrendering its bite, Wasserstein’s writing still lands.
This revival just can't decide how many of them to answer at once.
Unfortunately, Lichty’s performance was not up to the standards of her fellow performers.
This production won’t inspire other productions.
Like frosted tips and dial-up internet, An American Daughter emerges as another relic of the ’90s best consigned to that bygone era.
The well written piece should advance like a show of firecrackers and sparklers, a cousin to writing by whip-smart Aaron Sorkin. It rarely does.

La Femme's production never gets there. Instead, an unevenly cast company inhabits a handsome Georgetown living room while Wasserstein's ideas flicker around them, occasionally reminding us of the sharper, funnier and more provocative play this might have been.

cn.t: Wasserstein's 1997 political drama feels dated despite timely themes, with critics finding it a clunky period piece that pales against today's politics. Solid cast can't overcome meandering script.
